items.stem: A drug has a half-life of 6 hours. Approximately how long until it reaches steady state on regular dosing?

options.rationale: Correct: steady state is reached after roughly four to five half-lives, so about 24-30 hours.
One half-life removes only about half the drug; steady state needs several half-lives.
Time to steady state depends on half-life, not a fixed 72 hours.
A single dose cannot establish steady state during repeated dosing.

items.explanation: Correct: steady state is reached after roughly four to five half-lives, so about 24-30 hours.

items.stem: A competitive antagonist is given with an agonist. What is the characteristic effect on the agonist dose-response curve?

options.text: It shifts the curve to the right, and can be overcome by more agonist
options.rationale: Correct: competitive antagonism is surmountable, shifting the curve rightward without lowering the maximum.

options.text: It lowers the maximum response and cannot be overcome
options.rationale: That describes a non-competitive (irreversible) antagonist, not a competitive one.
An antagonist reduces apparent potency; it does not increase it.

options.text: It has no effect on the agonist
options.rationale: A competitive antagonist clearly reduces the agonist effect at a given dose.

items.explanation: Correct: competitive antagonism is surmountable, shifting the curve rightward without lowering the maximum.

items.stem: Which TWO factors would be expected to raise the plasma concentration of a renally cleared drug? (Select TWO)

options.rationale: Correct: impaired renal clearance reduces elimination and raises plasma levels.
Correct: displacement increases free drug in plasma.
Enzyme induction speeds metabolism and lowers concentration.
A larger volume of distribution tends to lower plasma concentration.

items.explanation: Correct: impaired renal clearance reduces elimination and raises plasma levels.
